patient.chief_complaint: Six weeks of progressive headaches and two focal seizures; new left-hand clumsiness
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Rajiv Mehta is a 38-year-old right-handed South Asian software engineer with no prior neurological history who presents with a six-week history of progressive frontal headaches, two witnessed focal seizures with left upper extremity jerking, and newly noticed clumsiness of his left hand. His headaches began insidiously approximately six weeks ago as a dull, diffuse frontal pressure that he initially attributed to stress related to a recent product launch at work. Unlike his usual tension-type headaches, these are present on awakening and have been increasing in intensity and duration over the past three weeks. He began taking over-the-counter ibuprofen with partial relief. Approximately three weeks ago, his wife noticed that he was repeatedly misplacing items and seeming slower in his thinking, which he discounted as work-related fatigue. Two days before admission, he experienced a witnessed episode at breakfast consisting of sustained rhythmic jerking of the left hand and forearm lasting approximately 90 seconds, followed by a brief period of confusion lasting approximately 5 minutes. He was brought to the local emergency department where levetiracetam was initiated. One day prior to transfer, he had a second similar episode despite levetiracetam, prompting transfer to the neurology service at this institution. He reports that over the past two weeks he has noticed intermittent clumsiness when typing with his left hand, which is non-dominant but still creates occupational difficulty. He denies any visual changes, language difficulty, nausea, vomiting, or fever. He has not lost consciousness. His wife reports no personality change. He has lost approximately 3 kg over the past six weeks, which he attributes to reduced appetite. He has no known history of cancer and no exposures to ionizing radiation or carcinogens beyond his prior smoking history, which he stopped a decade ago. An outpatient MRI obtained at the referring facility showed a right frontal mass with enhancement, prompting urgent transfer and admission.

results.title: The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
results.authors: Louis DN, Perry A, Wesseling P, et al.
results.key_finding: The 2021 WHO classification introduces IDH mutation status as the primary molecular determinant separating astrocytoma from glioblastoma. IDH-mutant astrocytoma grade 4 is classified separately from IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (grade 4) and has a distinct and more favorable prognosis. IDH-mutant astrocytoma requires IDH mutation, ATRX loss, absence of 1p/19q codeletion, and presence of grade 4 histological features (necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation). CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion also confers grade 4 designation to IDH-mutant astrocytoma even without histological grade 4 features.

results.title: Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma
results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.key_finding: Concurrent radiation (60 Gy in 30 fractions) with daily temozolomide (75 mg/m2) followed by adjuvant temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2, days 1-5, every 28 days for 6 cycles) improved median survival to 14.6 months vs 12.1 months in newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype GBM. This protocol is extrapolated to IDH-mutant grade 4 astrocytoma as well, pending dedicated trial data.

results.title: IDH-mutant astrocytoma grade 4: clinical behavior, molecular features, and treatment outcomes compared with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma
results.authors: Tesileanu CM, Dirven L, Wijnenga MM, et al.
results.key_finding: IDH-mutant grade 4 astrocytoma has a substantially more favorable prognosis than IDH-wildtype GBM (median OS approximately 24-30 months vs 15 months), tends to affect younger patients (median age ~40 years vs ~60 years for GBM), and frequently presents in the frontal lobe. Molecular profiling is essential because pre-operative imaging may not reliably distinguish IDH-mutant from IDH-wildtype high-grade glioma.

results.title: MGMT promoter methylation as a predictive biomarker for temozolomide benefit in high-grade glioma
results.authors: Hegi ME, Diserens AC, Gorlia T, et al.
results.key_finding: MGMT promoter methylation predicts benefit from temozolomide chemotherapy in high-grade glioma; methylated patients have significantly improved overall survival with concurrent chemoradiation. IDH-mutant tumors are commonly MGMT methylated.

output.summary: WHO 2021 CNS tumor classification defines IDH-mutant astrocytoma, grade 4 as a molecularly and biologically distinct entity from IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Diagnosis requires IDH mutation (typically IDH1 R132H), absence of 1p/19q codeletion, ATRX loss, and either histological grade 4 features (necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation) or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion. IDH-mutant grade 4 astrocytoma disproportionately affects younger adults (median ~40 years), favors the frontal lobe, and carries a substantially better prognosis than IDH-wildtype GBM (median OS 24-30 months). Standard treatment parallels that for high-grade gliomas: maximal safe resection followed by concurrent radiation and temozolomide. MGMT promoter methylation — common in IDH-mutant tumors — predicts enhanced benefit from temozolomide. Molecular profiling is essential because imaging cannot reliably distinguish IDH-mutant from IDH-wildtype high-grade glioma. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.recommendation: Neurosurgical consultation completed. The right frontal mass with partial ring enhancement, focal necrosis, elevated rCBV, and 4 mm midline shift is consistent with a high-grade glial neoplasm pending tissue diagnosis. The lesion is located in the right superior and middle frontal gyri with the posterior margin approaching the precentral gyrus. Neuronavigation-guided maximal safe resection is recommended as the initial procedure given the resectable location and relatively preserved neurological function. Extent of resection will be balanced against preservation of motor cortex and corticospinal tracts. Intraoperative neuromonitoring with cortical and subcortical stimulation mapping is planned. Tissue will be submitted for full molecular profiling per WHO 2021 (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT, ATRX, TERT, CDKN2A/B, EGFR).

output.proposed: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily (current); dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 hours (proposed for perioperative cerebral edema)
interactions: Levetiracetam + dexamethasone: No direct pharmacokinetic interaction. Dexamethasone does not significantly alter levetiracetam levels. Levetiracetam is preferred over enzyme-inducing AEDs (phenytoin, carbamazepine) in brain tumor patients receiving chemotherapy, as it does not induce CYP3A4 and therefore does not accelerate temozolomide metabolism.
Cetirizine: Mild additive sedation possible with levetiracetam; clinically minor at current doses.
warnings: Dexamethasone causes steroid-induced hyperglycemia; monitor blood glucose, particularly in the perioperative period
Prolonged dexamethasone use (>3-4 weeks) increases risk of steroid myopathy, adrenal suppression, and infection; taper to the lowest effective dose as edema resolves
Levetiracetam can cause behavioral side effects (irritability, mood changes); monitor and consider dose adjustment if significant
If temozolomide is subsequently initiated, enzyme-inducing AEDs should be avoided due to risk of reduced temozolomide exposure; levetiracetam is the preferred choice (no CYP3A4 induction)
Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is required if concurrent chemoradiation is initiated
alternatives: Lacosamide — alternative non-enzyme-inducing AED if levetiracetam is not tolerated
Lamotrigine — alternative, but has slower titration
Methylprednisolone — alternative corticosteroid if dexamethasone is not available

critical_actions: Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) as the primary diagnostic step before any invasive procedure
Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (maximal safe resection with neuronavigation and intraoperative neuromonitoring) and operative planning

Submit surgical specimen for full WHO 2021 molecular profiling: IDH1/2, ATRX, 1p/19q, MGMT, TERT, EGFR, CDKN2A/B — the IDH mutation status is the single most important molecular distinction for prognosis and management

contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture given the mass effect and midline shift — herniation risk

Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis and molecular profiling are complete — IDH status determines the correct diagnosis and guides prognosis
Do not substitute enzyme-inducing AEDs (phenytoin, carbamazepine) for levetiracetam — CYP3A4 induction would accelerate temozolomide clearance and reduce chemotherapy efficacy

Do not conclude IDH-wildtype glioblastoma based on imaging alone in a patient of this age with a frontal tumor — molecular profiling is mandatory per WHO 2021 and the IDH-mutant diagnosis carries substantially different prognosis
key_reasoning_points: WHO 2021 establishes IDH mutation status as the defining molecular criterion separating astrocytoma from glioblastoma — a right frontal high-grade glioma in a 38-year-old must undergo molecular profiling before a diagnosis of glioblastoma is accepted

IDH-mutant astrocytoma grade 4 is molecularly distinct from IDH-wildtype GBM: younger demographic (median ~40 years), frontal predilection, better prognosis (median OS ~24-30 months vs ~15 months), and commonly MGMT methylated — features all present in this case

The combination of IDH1 R132H mutation (positive IHC), ATRX loss, absent 1p/19q codeletion, and histological grade 4 features (microvascular proliferation and focal necrosis) establishes the integrated WHO 2021 diagnosis of astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4

MGMT promoter methylation (61%) in IDH-mutant grade 4 astrocytoma predicts enhanced benefit from temozolomide chemotherapy — an important prognostic and predictive marker to communicate to neuro-oncology

red_herrings.data_point: 38-year-old patient with frontal lobe mass, less florid ring enhancement, limited necrosis, and new-onset seizures — constellation that anchors toward a lower-grade IDH-mutant glioma (WHO grade 2 or 3)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Younger age and somewhat less aggressive imaging (incomplete ring enhancement, small focal necrosis compared to classical GBM) may lead an agent to anchor on a lower-grade IDH-mutant glioma and defer or under-prioritize tissue diagnosis
